title: A Conservative Loss Recovery Algorithm Based on Selective Acknowledgment (SACK)
summary: This RFC presents a conservative loss recovery algorithm for TCP using the SACK option. It follows the congestion control rules in RFC 5681 while allowing senders to recover better when several segments are lost from one flight of data. It obsoletes RFC 3517.

eli5.summary: When several pieces of a message are lost, the receiver lists exactly which ones arrived. The sender can resend only the missing ones.

questions: how does tcp sack loss recovery work
what is a rescue retransmission in tcp
subtitle: A conservative way for TCP senders to use SACK information to recover several lost segments in one flight.

tldr.problem: TCP senders often ignore the information in SACK blocks when deciding what to retransmit, and RFC 3517 left several situations unhandled.
tldr.mechanism: The sender keeps a scoreboard of SACKed data, estimates the bytes still in the network (pipe), and uses NextSeg() to pick what to send while following RFC 5681 congestion control.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6675 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3517, adding duplicate ACK counting from SACK data, a rescue retransmission and a refined loss test.

facts.label: Rescue retransmission
facts.value: One per entry into loss recovery, up to 1 SMSS

facts.label: IsLost byte test
facts.value: More than (DupThresh - 1) * SMSS bytes SACKed above

today: RFC 6675 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 3517. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC presents a loss recovery algorithm for TCP built on the selective acknowledgment (SACK) option from RFC 2018. The option was being steadily deployed, yet there was evidence that hosts did not use the SACK information when making retransmission and congestion control decisions. The goal is to outline one straightforward way to use it.

RFC 5681 allows advanced loss recovery as long as it follows the spirit of TCP's congestion control, and RFC 6582 describes one such method, NewReno. The algorithm here is heavily based on work by Fall and Floyd and is a conservative replacement of the fast recovery algorithm. Other SACK-based methods are allowed if they follow RFC 5681. The decisions about what to send are largely decoupled from congestion control, so they can be treated as separate issues.

It is a revision of RFC 3517 that addresses situations that document did not handle explicitly.
sections.eli5: The receiver already tells the sender which pieces arrived. This RFC shows the sender how to actually use that list.

sections.title: Definitions and the Scoreboard
sections.content:
The sender stores six variables. HighACK is the highest byte cumulatively acknowledged. HighData is the highest sequence number sent. HighRxt is the highest sequence number retransmitted in the current recovery. RescueRxt is the highest sequence number optimistically retransmitted to keep the ACK clock going when the loss is at the end of the window and no new data is available. Pipe estimates the bytes outstanding in the network. DupAcks counts duplicate acknowledgments since the last cumulative one.

Here a duplicate acknowledgment is a segment carrying a SACK block that identifies previously unacknowledged and un-SACKed octets between HighACK and HighData. This differs from RFC 5681: an ACK with new SACK data counts even if it carries new data, changes the window or moves the cumulative point. DupThresh is the number of duplicate ACKs needed to trigger a retransmission, 3 per RFC 5681.

The sender keeps a per-connection data structure called the scoreboard. Its details are out of scope, but it must be able to mark arbitrary sequence number ranges as selectively acknowledged. SACKed data MUST NOT leave the retransmission buffer until it is cumulatively acknowledged, because SACK information is advisory.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps a checklist of what the receiver has confirmed, plus a few counters to track what is still on the way.

sections.title: The Scoreboard Routines
sections.content:
The scoreboard SHOULD provide four functions. Update() marks cumulatively ACKed and SACKed octets. IsLost(SeqNum) returns true when DupThresh discontiguous SACKed sequences have arrived above SeqNum, or more than (DupThresh - 1) * SMSS bytes above it have been SACKed. SetPipe() walks from HighACK to HighData and counts octets that are not SACKed and not deemed lost, plus retransmitted octets up to HighRxt.

NextSeg() picks what to send next, by these rules in order:

  1. The smallest un-SACKed sequence number above HighRxt, below the highest SACKed octet, and judged lost: send one segment of up to SMSS octets from there. This is a MUST.
  2. Otherwise, new data from HighData+1 if there is any and the receiver's window allows. This is a MUST.
  3. Otherwise, a segment from an un-SACKed number meeting the position tests but not the IsLost test. This is a SHOULD.
  4. Otherwise, a single rescue retransmission per entry into loss recovery, covering the highest outstanding un-SACKed sequence number, if HighACK is greater than RescueRxt. This is also a SHOULD.
  5. Otherwise, NextSeg() reports failure.

Rules 3 and 4 are a last resort. They help sustain the ACK clock and may avoid retransmission timeouts, but they put two copies of the same data in the network, so the sender may underestimate pipe.
sections.eli5: The sender first resends what is surely lost, then sends new pieces, and only as a last resort re-sends something it is merely suspicious about.

sections.title: Entering, Running and Leaving Loss Recovery
sections.content:
On every ACK with SACK information the scoreboard MUST be updated, and a cumulative ACK resets DupAcks to zero. If the ACK is a duplicate by this RFC's definition and the sender is not in recovery, DupAcks is increased and the sender checks two triggers. Recovery starts if DupAcks has reached DupThresh, or if IsLost(HighACK + 1) is true, meaning enough segments have arrived above the cumulative point. Otherwise the sender MAY send new data under Limited Transmit, limited by pipe and cwnd.

To enter recovery the sender sets RecoveryPoint = HighData, sets ssthresh and cwnd to FlightSize / 2 as RFC 5681 requires, retransmits the first segment presumed dropped, sets HighRxt and RescueRxt to its highest sequence number, and runs SetPipe().

While in recovery, a cumulative ACK above RecoveryPoint ends it. For any other ACK the sender updates the scoreboard and recomputes pipe. If cwnd - pipe is at least 1 SMSS, it SHOULD query NextSeg() and send segments, updating HighRxt, HighData and pipe, and repeat while room remains. This can send a burst of back-to-back segments.
sections.eli5: When enough gaps show up, the sender slows down a bit and starts patching holes. It stops when everything sent before the trouble has been confirmed.

sections.title: Timeouts and the RTO Timer
sections.content:
A receiver may discard data it has already SACKed, so RFC 2018 suggests a sender SHOULD expunge SACK information after a retransmission timeout (RTO). This RFC does not change that, but notes that some view it as too strong and that implementers should check for updates. A SACK sender SHOULD use all SACK information made available during recovery after an RTO.

If an RTO occurs during recovery, RecoveryPoint MUST be set to HighData, the algorithm MUST be terminated, and a new recovery MUST NOT start until HighACK reaches the new RecoveryPoint. NextSeg() is not appropriate after an RTO; filling in the reported gaps is a reasonable approach.

Because this algorithm can keep the ACK clock running through a long loss event, the standard RFC 6298 timer, which re-arms when the cumulative ACK advances, may expire prematurely. Implementers may instead re-arm the timer on each retransmission sent during recovery. This is more conservative and may prevent needless retransmissions and further reduction of the congestion window.
sections.eli5: If the sender waits too long with no news, it starts over carefully. A slightly patient timer can stop it from resending things that are already on their way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The algorithm shares the security considerations of RFC 5681. A key difference is that SACK-based recovery is more robust against attackers who forge duplicate ACKs to force the sender to cut cwnd, since SACK gives the sender an additional check on whether an ACK is legitimate. The RFC says this is not fool-proof.

It also mitigates a blind attack sketched in a CPNI technical note, where an attacker spoofs out-of-window data so the endpoint sends duplicate cumulative ACKs. Requiring SACK information to trigger recovery helps because those duplicate ACKs will not show reception of previously un-SACKed in-window data.
sections.eli5: A forged 'I missed something' message is easy to fake, but a precise list of which pieces arrived is much harder to fake.

sections.title: Changes Relative to RFC 3517
sections.content:
RFC 6675 makes these changes to RFC 3517:

  • The DupAcks variable is added, and its use specified.
  • The IsLost() test now needs more than (DupThresh - 1) * SMSS octets SACKed above a number, instead of at least DupThresh * SMSS. At least three segments after the number must still be SACKed, but loss detection improves when outstanding segments are smaller than SMSS.
  • The definition of a duplicate acknowledgment now uses SACK information, so loss recovery can be entered on SACK evidence of three segments above a gap. RFC 3517 used that idea only during recovery.
  • The RescueRxt variable is added, allowing one extra retransmission per entry into recovery, of no more than 1 SMSS.
  • NextSeg() rule 3 changes from MAY to SHOULD.
sections.eli5: This update fixes a few gaps in the older version: how to count missing pieces, one last-chance resend, and a firmer rule for when to try risky resends.

items.title: HighRxt
items.text: Highest sequence number retransmitted in this recovery.

items.title: RescueRxt
items.text: Highest optimistically retransmitted number, used to keep the ACK clock going.

items.title: Pipe
items.text: Estimate of bytes outstanding in the network.

items.title: DupAcks
items.text: Duplicate ACKs since the last cumulative ACK.
